profiles.meeting_scenario: A defense-side planning meeting at a law firm representing a national grocery delivery platform in an antitrust class action. Plaintiffs' economist has served an expert report claiming classwide overcharge based on 180 million transaction records, lasso-selected controls, and a gradient-boosted pricing model. The meeting is between the lead antitrust partner and the firm's e-discovery/data-analytics counsel to plan the next six weeks before expert discovery closes: what to request from opposing counsel, what to collect internally, how to support the rebuttal economist, and when to begin drafting a possible Daubert motion. The agenda is to align on the discovery asks, the internal data workstream, the handoff to the rebuttal expert, and the filing timeline. The expected outcome is a concrete task plan assigning responsibility for the replication materials, data provenance work, expert support, and motion-preparation milestones.

members.name: Rachel Kim
members.expertise: Class certification strategy, expert discovery, Daubert motions, antitrust economics in litigation
members.background: Rachel is a senior partner who has led multiple pricing and platform antitrust cases and regularly works with outside economists, but she delegates technical data handling to specialists and focuses on record-building and court-facing strategy.
members.private_state: She wants a defensible, efficient plan that gives the rebuttal expert enough to undermine plaintiffs' model without opening unnecessary discovery fights or expanding the record into consulting-expert materials she thinks the court may not require.
hidden_assumptions: A 'replication package' means the materials needed for the rebuttal expert to rerun the headline model reported by the testifying economist, not every upstream preprocessing step.
When people refer to the 'raw data,' they usually mean the transaction tables already produced in litigation, because those are the operative business records the expert relied on.
Asking to 'document the variable selection process' should be limited to what the testifying expert considered or used, not notebooks or scripts from consultants who shaped the inputs earlier.
If the team can identify a few plausible reliability gaps and preserve them cleanly, that is already 'enough for Daubert' even if the model is not fully reverse-engineered.

members.name: Daniel Ortega
members.expertise: Structured data collections, data provenance, forensic defensibility, expert support for statistical and machine-learning evidence
members.background: Daniel is a counsel-level specialist who bridges litigation teams and technical vendors; he has worked on matters involving large transactional datasets, source-to-report tracing, and reproducibility challenges to expert models.
members.private_state: He wants the plan to force a technically complete record so the rebuttal economist can test how the plaintiffs' result changes with different preprocessing and feature-engineering choices, and he is worried that a narrow request set will leave the team unable to prove instability later.
hidden_assumptions: A 'replication package' means an end-to-end reproducibility bundle including ingestion logic, cleaning rules, feature engineering, code versions, and training/evaluation splits.

When people say 'raw data,' they mean the source merchant-feed files before normalization, deduplication, and platform-side harmonization, because those transformations can materially affect model outputs.

To 'document the variable selection process,' the team needs the upstream scripts, notebooks, and intermediate feature lists that fed the final expert model, even if they originated with non-testifying analysts.
Something is 'enough for Daubert' only if the team can technically demonstrate instability, leakage, or irreproducibility rather than merely point to theoretical gaps.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to ask for a 'replication package' from plaintiffs.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the files, code, and report exhibits necessary for the rebuttal economist to rerun the final reported model and damages outputs.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a full end-to-end reproducibility package including preprocessing, feature engineering, variable-selection routines, software versions, and train/test splits.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In expert-discovery practice, 'replication package' sounds like standard shorthand, so each hears a familiar phrase and assumes the other shares their professional default about what replication naturally includes.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the raw transaction data
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to getting or tracing the 'raw data' behind the economist's model.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the monthly transaction tables already produced in the case and cited in the expert report.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the original merchant-feed and platform-ingestion files before they were standardized into litigation tables.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are discussing the same model and same dataset history, and 'raw data' is a common umbrella term; because neither needs to name a file path or system at the meeting, the reference gap feels invisible.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they need plaintiffs to 'document the variable selection process.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this covers materials the testifying economist actually reviewed or relied on when choosing the controls reported in the final analysis.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this includes earlier notebooks, consultant scripts, discarded candidate features, and data-science work that narrowed the feature set before the expert ever saw it.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds precise enough on the surface because both care about the same model-building history, yet they silently draw the boundary at different stages of that history based on their legal versus technical habits.

misalignment_points.topic: Threshold for being ready to draft Daubert
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they want to know when they have 'enough for Daubert.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks they are ready once they can articulate a credible reliability challenge tied to missing documentation or opaque feature selection, even if the model is not fully reproduced.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks they are ready only once the rebuttal team can run meaningful stress tests showing the result materially changes under reasonable alternative preprocessing or feature choices.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Lawyers often use 'enough for Daubert' as a shared strategic benchmark, but trial-facing and technical-support roles import different standards of sufficiency without feeling any need to spell them out.

turns.inner_thought: We have six weeks, so I need a lean, court-facing plan. The rebuttal economist needs enough to rerun the final reported overcharge model and identify a few defensible reliability problems. I do not want to turn this into a fishing expedition over every consultant-side preprocessing decision or trigger a side fight about consulting-expert materials. If we can show opacity around inputs or controls and frame that cleanly, that may already be enough for Daubert.
turns.utterance: Let me frame the next six weeks. We need to support our rebuttal economist in a disciplined way and make an early judgment about whether we'll have enough for Daubert. So I'd like us to come out of this with four things: what we ask plaintiffs for, what we pull together internally, how we tee this up for the expert, and when we start drafting.

turns.inner_thought: The key is not just getting final exhibits or a runnable endpoint. We need an end-to-end reproducibility record: ingestion, cleaning, feature engineering, versions, splits, and how the model moved from source inputs to outputs. If we don't get that now, we may never be able to show instability later. A complete replication package is the first gate.
turns.utterance: I agree. The first priority, in my view, is getting a complete replication package from plaintiffs so we can map the model from input data all the way through to the reported outputs. Without that, everything else is guesswork.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll put Daniel on the requests because he knows the technical asks, but I want the scope grounded in what the rebuttal economist actually needs to rerun the headline model promptly. We do not need to boil the ocean. If he brings me a focused list that gets us the files, code, and supporting materials tied to the final analysis, that's the right balance. And if those materials reveal obvious gaps, we can move toward enough for Daubert quickly.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. Why don't you draft the request list on the replication package, and let's keep it oriented toward what the rebuttal expert needs to rerun the headline overcharge model quickly. If we can get that moving fast, we'll be in a much better position to assess whether we have enough for Daubert.

turns.inner_thought: I need to make sure the ask reaches back before the litigation tables. The real risk is that the reported model sits on standardized data that already embeds judgment calls. If we don't pin down the source merchant feeds and the transformations before those tables, we won't know what changed or whether preprocessing drove the result. I'll say raw data lineage and flag the path into the report tables.
turns.utterance: I also want to pin down the raw data lineage. In particular, I think we should understand the path into the tables cited in the report and any transformations along the way, because that affects how confidently we can evaluate what the model is actually using.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds manageable enough. They already produced the transaction tables, and those are what I expect the economist relied on. We can treat those productions as the raw data for our purposes and use them as the starting point for expert support. I do not want to suggest we need to reopen discovery into every system upstream unless we later see a concrete reason.
turns.utterance: Yes, tracing the raw data should be manageable. They've already produced the transaction tables, and those are the obvious starting point for supporting our expert. If we anchor the work there and then identify any breaks in the chain, that should give us a clean record.

turns.inner_thought: We also need the full model-building history, not just the final controls list. With lasso and boosted models, the choices before the final run matter—screening, engineered features, discarded candidates, and narrowing steps. If those sit in notebooks or scripts from analysts, that's exactly where instability may show up. I'll keep it high-level: document the variable selection process, including how things were screened and narrowed before training.
turns.utterance: The other piece I'd put near the top of the list is making sure they document the variable selection process. Given the way they've described the model, I want materials that show how features were screened, engineered, and narrowed before the final model was trained.

turns.inner_thought: I'm aligned on asking them to document the variable selection process, but I want the request tethered to the testifying economist's work: what he considered, what explains the controls in the report, and what he relied on. That's discoverable and useful. I do not want an overbroad demand for every consultant draft or experimental path that invites objections and delay.
turns.utterance: Agreed, we do need them to document the variable selection process. Let's frame that around what the testifying economist considered and the materials that explain the controls that appear in the report. If we can tie it to the analysis they actually served, that will be easier to defend.

turns.inner_thought: Once the replication package arrives, I want the vendor and our team to reconstruct the full pipeline so the rebuttal economist can run sensitivity checks on preprocessing and feature choices. That's the only way I'll feel we can prove instability rather than just speculate. We should be ready to absorb code, intermediate data, and lineage materials immediately.
turns.utterance: On our side, I'd propose a parallel workstream with the vendor so that, as soon as the replication package comes in, we can rebuild the pipeline and support sensitivity checks. That way the rebuttal expert isn't waiting on us once production lands.

turns.inner_thought: I need a midpoint checkpoint, not an endless technical exercise. By then I want to know whether we can articulate the main reliability problems—missing documentation, opacity around controls, any inability to rerun the reported analysis. If yes, drafting should start immediately, even if Daniel still wants deeper testing. Enough for Daubert does not require complete reverse engineering in my mind.
turns.utterance: Good. Let's put a midpoint deadline on that. In about three weeks, I want you to tell me whether we have enough for Daubert, and if the main reliability gaps are visible by then, I want drafting to begin right away rather than waiting until the very end.

turns.inner_thought: I'll take that as: build the record fast and see whether we can get to actual stress testing by midstream. My task list is clear from my perspective—secure the full replication package, trace the raw data back through its lineage, and gather all materials needed to document the variable selection process. If we can get the pipeline rebuilt in time, the rebuttal economist can test whether the result moves under reasonable alternatives, which is what I consider enough for Daubert.
turns.utterance: Understood. I'll handle the request list around the replication package, get the raw data path traced, and assemble what we need to document the variable selection process. In parallel I'll stand up the vendor workstream so the rebuttal expert can start stress-testing the model as soon as materials come in, and I'll report back at the midpoint on whether we're at enough for Daubert.
